teaser.en: Termites leave its wood alone, so coastal builders reach for this spiny, layered tree when they need house poles that last.

summary.en: *Mwanga kululu* is a spiny Terminalia of the coastal bushland, with branches spread in neat horizontal tiers. Its termite-resistant wood is cut for house poles and dhow keels, and the Digo of Diani use its bark against malaria.

about.en:
*Mwanga kululu* grows into a tree of up to 15 m with a distinctive layered shape: its branches stand out horizontally in tiers, and the young shoots zig-zag from one bud to the next. Stout spines arm the branches. The leaves are small, notched at the tip, and gathered in tight clusters on short side-shoots, which gives the tree a tufted look.

In flower it carries slender spikes of small pink-white blossoms. Like other Terminalias, it then sets small, flattened winged fruits.

where.en: It grows in coastal bushland and wooded grassland, often on rocky ground. Its tiered silhouette makes it one of the easier bush trees to pick out from a distance.

uses.en:
The wood is hard and resistant to termites, and it is increasingly used for house poles at the coast. It is also cut for dhow keels, and carved into stools and household utensils.

The Digo of Diani take a cold-water infusion of the stem bark to treat malaria.

culture.en: The tree is believed to have magical properties. Its other name, *mwanga*, is shared with the river terminalia, which the Digo connect with a spirit called Mwanga.

names.en: In Digo it is *mwanga kululu*, or simply *mwanga*. Swahili speakers call it *mwanga* or *mwangati*, and in Giriama it is *mwanga*. The English name is spiny terminalia. The short form *mwanga* is also the Digo name for the river terminalia (*Terminalia sambesiaca*), so the longer *mwanga kululu* helps tell the two apart.

conservation.en: Rising demand for termite-proof house poles puts more pressure on this tree than it once faced.

reason.en: River terminalia, same genus and same short name
Violet tree, also used against malaria in Diani
